name: Khezha Naga
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Kapfo, Kedutso. 2005. The Ethnology of the Khezhas and the Khezha Grammar. Mysore: CIIL (410pp); also Kapfo 1992 Khezha: A Descriptive Analysis (PhD, 386pp)
earlier_scan.note: Full CIIL grammar plausibly covers prosody (Kapfo 1989 treats tone); no digital copy found

new_statements.quote: Khezha may be referred as a nonrestricted level tone language, because, pitch of syllable does not rise or fall at the time of production in this language. Even in the pattern of their combination, various tones can freely be assigned to any individual syllables without restricting the number of occurrence throughout the entire word. [...] That is, every syllable in Khezha has a tone and there is always a one-to-one correlation between the number of syllables and the number of tones in every utterance. For instance, só 'repeat', so 'drink', still sò 'count', 'bribe'. [...] They do not differ in length or intensity from other syllables, but their contrast is manifested solely by pitch. Presently I have identified three primary tones in this language.
new_statements.citation: Kapfo, Kedutso. 2005. The Ethnology of the Khezhas and the Khezha Grammar. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages.
new_statements.locator: Part II, ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.9 Tones / 2.9.1 Contrastive Tones in Khezha, pp. 93-94 (PDF pages 111-112 of the archive.org text PDF)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Khezha is described as a level-tone language with three lexical tones (high, mid, low) on every syllable, assigned freely to any syllable of the word; the grammar contains no statement of word stress or accent at all. The only remark bearing on stress is that tonally contrasting syllables differ neither in length nor in intensity, only in pitch. No stress position is stated; the language should be treated as tonal with no reported word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. For tone: the e- noun prefix normally carries low tone (Kapfo 1989: 68); allotones (H ~ HM, L ~ LM) and tone sandhi rules under compounding are given in 2.9.2-2.9.3 (pp. 95-97).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable level (lexical tone on every syllable of every utterance); examples are citation forms of monosyllabic and disyllabic words. Both Kapfo works describe the author's own Pfutsero (Letromi) village dialect; Kapfo 1989 p. 67 notes each Khezha village has its own dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Kapfo sources describe the author's native Pfutsero/Letromi village dialect of Khezha (Kapfo 1989: 67 'Pfutsero dialect'; Kapfo 2005: 92 'my village dialect Letromi'), with village-level dialect variation noted. Glottolog khez1235 = Khezha Naga; Wikipedia now files the language as 'Kuzhami' (the autonym in Kapfo's 2007 dictionary title Kuzhale-Chahale). Glottolog 5.3's langdoc page for khez1235 appears to point at nekk1240, suggesting a recent reorganisation of the languoid; no separate dialect glottocode identified.

sources.note: No stress or accent section; the phonology chapter has no word for 'stress' at all. Sec. 2.9.1 (p. 94) says every syllable carries one of three level tones (H/M/L), that minimal sets 'do not differ in length or intensity from other syllables, but their contrast is manifested solely by pitch', and that Khezha is a 'nonrestricted level tone language' where tones are assigned freely to any syllable of the word (pp. 93-94). Sec. 2.8 (p. 91) says the language is open-syllabic and nouns are minimally disyllabic (e- prefix on monosyllabic roots).

sources.citation: Kapfo, Kedutso. 1989. Tones in Khezha noun constructions. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 12(2): 67-78. DOI 10.15144/LTBA-12.2.67
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (grep of scanned for stress, accent, intensity, prominence, loud: no hits). States (p. 67-68) that Khezha is a tone language with three levels H/M/L; 'Tone is an obligatory feature of the syllable; every syllable occurs with a tone'; the e- prefix 'occurs simply to give greater phonological weight to the attached syllable' and normally carries low tone; describes tone alternations in noun compounding/derivation (Pfutsero dialect).

sources.citation: Kapfo, Kedutso. 2007. Kuzhale-Chahale Dikshüneri: Khezha-English Dictionary. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. xxvi+547 pp.
sources.note: scanned text searched: no stress/accent statement; only a note under the entry 'hi' that 'there are three (3) syllable tones in Khezha: high, mid and low' governing the hi/hy allomorphy.
